key_insight: HorizonMath shows that language models can be evaluated on novel, research-like mathematical problems by pairing a large benchmark of mostly-unsolved problems with an automated verification framework, enabling objective measurement of discovery-oriented capabilities.
problem_solved: Lack of standardized, verifiable benchmarks for assessing whether AI models can make progress on important, predominantly unsolved problems in computational and applied mathematics.
method: Curate a benchmark of 100+ predominantly unsolved problems spanning 8 domains in computational and applied math.
Provide an open-source evaluation pipeline that automatically verifies model outputs using computational checks and formal/numeric verification tools.
Run and analyze model attempts to generate solutions, using the verifier to classify correct/partial/incorrect results and produce reproducible evidence.
impact: Enables rigorous, reproducible measurement of AI progress toward mathematical discovery and gives practitioners a toolset to benchmark, debug, and improve models on research-grade tasks. This lowers the barrier to evaluating and iterating on models aimed at scientific and mathematical reasoning.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: Model -> Proposed Result -> Automated Verifier (symbolic/numeric/formal) -> Pass/Fail/Partial
Benchmark summary chart: number of problems by domain (8-domain breakdown) and difficulty
Examples panel: side-by-side examples of a model proposal, verification steps, and final status
Metric dashboard mockup: verification success rate, partial credit, and reproducibility indicators
paper_title: HorizonMath: Measuring AI Progress Toward Mathematical Discovery with Automatic Verification
paper_authors: Erik Y. Wang, Sumeet Motwani, James V. Roggeveen, Eliot Hodges, Dulhan Jayalath
